passage: On her second day as lead, Damini booked ten minutes with each person at the pantry table. "What do you enjoy? What are you good at?" Chirag liked talking to customers. Rutuja enjoyed tidy screen work. Nilesh, who barely spoke in meetings, came alive when asked about databases and talked for twenty minutes. Damini gave the database work to Nilesh and the customer calls to Chirag. Rather than looking over every change people made, she held a ten-minute check-in each Monday. By week three the database work was done ahead of schedule. Nilesh sent a short message: "Can I take the reporting part too?" She read it twice and smiled.

qa.q: How long were the Monday check-ins?
qa.a: Each Monday check-in lasted ten minutes.

qa.q: What might Nilesh have felt when asked about databases?
qa.a: Nilesh probably felt keen and appreciated, coming alive and talking for twenty minutes after barely speaking in meetings.

qa.q: What could Damini do if some task matched nobody's strengths, and why?
qa.a: Damini could rotate it or pair two people on it, because sharing an unwanted job keeps the load fair while everyone learns something.

qa.q: How might Chirag see the way tasks were handed out?
qa.a: Chirag probably feels trusted and pleased to be doing the customer calls, since that matches what Chirag enjoys.

grounding: Illustrates a lead asking each member about their strengths, assigning work to match, and using short weekly check-ins instead of watching every commit.

passage:
"So, Ujjwal, what do you actually enjoy?" Jomon asked, pulling his chair closer in the small meeting room.
Ujjwal looked surprised. "Me? The database stuff. Queries, indexes. I like quiet problems."
"You never said so in stand-ups."
"Nobody asked."
Jomon wrote it down. He'd been asking each of the five this week. "Revathi likes front-end. Rakesh loves talking to clients. You like databases. So the schema and all the queries are yours."
"All of it?"
"All of it. I won't look at every commit. We'll do ten minutes every Thursday. You tell me what's done, what's stuck, what you need."
Ujjwal nodded slowly. "Just ten minutes?"
"If it's going well, ten minutes is plenty."
Three weeks later, at their Thursday check-in, Ujjwal showed him a query that had gone from twelve seconds to under one. He was almost smiling.

qa.q: How long are Jomon's weekly check-ins with Ujjwal?
qa.a: They are ten minutes every Thursday.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel when Jomon asked what he enjoyed?
qa.a: He felt surprised, since nobody had asked before, and later almost proud as he showed his faster query.

qa.q: What else could Jomon do if a strength-based task stalls?
qa.a: He could use the Thursday check-in to ask what help is needed, instead of taking the task back.

qa.q: How does Jomon's approach look to Ujjwal?
qa.a: Ujjwal feels trusted to own quiet work he enjoys, without someone watching every commit.

grounding: Shows a lead asking each member what they enjoy, giving database work to the quiet backend person and keeping short weekly check-ins.

passage:
My first month as team lead, I tried to watch everything. I checked every code change, rewrote comments, answered every question within minutes. By week four I was exhausted and the team was quieter than ever.
My friend Zubin, who'd led teams longer, asked me, "Do you even know what each of them likes doing?"
I didn't. So I asked. One by one, over tea. Anil lit up talking about design. Rohini loved testing. And Kiran, who barely spoke in meetings, said, "Honestly? Databases. I could tune queries all day."
So I gave Kiran the whole data layer. Anil got the interface, Rohini the testing plan. I stopped reviewing every commit and set up a ten-minute check-in with each of them on Wednesdays.
Two months in, Kiran presented the database design to the client. I'd never heard Kiran talk that long. I'm Pema, and I learned that trust gets more done than watching.

qa.q: Which task did Pema give to Kiran?
qa.a: Pema gave Kiran the whole data layer.

qa.q: How did Pema feel by week four of watching everything?
qa.a: Pema felt exhausted, and the team had become quieter than ever.

qa.q: What else could Pema do to keep the delegation working?
qa.a: Pema could use the Wednesday check-ins to ask what each person needs, stepping in only when someone is stuck.

qa.q: How might Kiran have felt presenting to the client?
qa.a: Kiran likely felt nervous but proud, speaking at length about work Kiran truly enjoyed and owned.

grounding: Shows a lead asking each member what they enjoy, giving database work to the quiet backend person and replacing close watching with short weekly check-ins.
